title: Pops Foster, bus seat-mate and old-looking young man
summary: Pops Foster looked sixty-five but had young energy; Holmes was his bus seat-mate and later exchanged Christmas cards with his wife Alma.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Boy, you're taking me way back a whole lot of years. You make me...
But that Russell band must have been something special, though, because you stuck together, you knew each other, and as you've mentioned, the music...
We enjoyed working with one another. You know what I mean? There was nobody in the organization that was mad with somebody else, you know, in the organization. We all enjoyed working together.

And Pops Foster was... Let me see. Pops Foster was supposed... He was the bass player. He came to New York in 1929. I was 19 years old when he come here. Pops Foster was supposed to be 65 years old when he joined the band. Well, I don't know how old Pops was. He looked to be 65. But whatever his age was, he had more life in him than I ever had in me, and I wasn't but 19 years old. And Pops and I used to run around together! And everybody liked Pops Foster. Everybody! He was just one of them old men... He wasn't all that old either, but he looked old.
He was 38. Because he was born in 1892.
He don't know when he was born. How would he know? But anyway, he was one of them old-looking men... I say, old-looking...

Because we'd go different places, and "Pops Foster, Pops..." -- everybody wants Pops, Pops... They think he was an old man too. He looked old. He was supposed to be 65 years old. And that's what I thought, too. Well, you could be right with that 38, because ain't no way in the world an old man 65 years old had the get up and go like he had. I mean, he had an old look on him, but he had a devilish head. His head had devilish ideas in it -- a younger man, you know?

Yeah, Pops was somethin' great. And him and I, because I was the baby in the band and he was the old man... And him and I, we were seat-mates on the bus. And boy, he was something else. Pops was a great old man.
A funny thing. I seen Pops almost fifty years later, maybe not that many years but it seemed like it to me, and he was telling me... He passed by my house one day when I was looking out the window, I stopped him, and we got to talking. And he was telling me, he said, "You know..." At that time, he was living in California, but he happened to be in New York working. He said, "You know something, Charlie?" He said, "I'm playing down there on Eighth Avenue (or in the Bronx, someplace) with some of my people, and I've got a whole lot of grandchildren around me. All my

grandchildren." I got to thinking, "What kind of children is he talkin' about?" I never heard of him havin' no children, period! And he was telling me he had so many grandchildren around, and then this-that-and-the-other... I said, "Yeah, Pops, it's all in the mind. All in the mind." [LAUGHS]
But Pops, he was great. He was a fine person. He finally passed away [1969], but his wife, I think she's still living.
I've got to send her a Christmas card this year. We got to sending one another Christmas cards, oh, I'd say about eight or ten years ago.

And of course, last year I didn't send her a card, because Liscotte(?) passed away during the year, and I didn't send out any Christmas cards at all. So as far as I'm concerned, she don't know that Liscotte(?) has passed away. I don't know if she knows or not. I guess so. But I'll send her a card this year, if she's still around to receive it. Nice person, Alma. Very nice.
